summary: A revision of the Data Transfer Protocol from RFC 171, written by the file transfer committee. It changes sequence number sizes, clarifies modes available messages and code assignments, then restates the whole protocol. It was updated by RFC 310 and replaced by RFC 354.

plainLanguage.summary: The Data Transfer Protocol defines ways to divide a connection's data into transactions. It also assigns types to control messages used by applications.

subtitle: Revises the Data Transfer Protocol for delimiting data and control transactions.

tldr.problem: Different ARPANET applications needed common ways to separate data into logical blocks and distinguish data from control information.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol defines three transfer modes and transaction types for handshakes, separators, errors, aborts and no-ops.
tldr.outcome: RFC 264 revised RFC 171, was updated by RFC 310 and was obsoleted by RFC 354.

sections.title: A Shared Data Transfer Mechanism
sections.content:
RFC 264 defines a Data Transfer Protocol (DTP) for applications such as remote job entry, file transfer, network mail, graphics and terminal communication. It separates data transfer from application functions to allow greater implementation flexibility and reduce protocol proliferation.

DTP defines logical transactions, separation of data and control information, and some error-control mechanisms. It does not define a data-transfer service or an initial connection protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: DTP is a lower-level mechanism that applications can use to delimit data and control messages. Each application decides how to use that mechanism.

sections.title: Three Ways to Delimit Transactions
sections.content:
DTP defines three transfer modes. An indefinite bit stream ends when the connection closes. Transparent block mode ends at a DLE ETX sequence; the sender doubles DLE bytes in the data and the receiver removes the extra one. Descriptor-and-count mode begins with a descriptor containing separate counts of information and filler bits.

Applications may mix modes on a connection. They may support a subset, and a handshake can exchange which receive modes are available.
sections.plainLanguage: A transaction can end when a connection closes, at an escape sequence or according to counts in a descriptor. The application protocol chooses which modes it uses.

sections.title: Types, Separators and Error Messages
sections.content:
The first 8-bit byte of each transaction specifies its type. Types B0 through B2 describe data modes; B8 through BA are corresponding control modes. Other types cover mode availability, information separators, error codes, aborts and no-ops.

Information separators can mark units, records, groups or files. Sequence numbers can help identify missing transactions, but DTP does not require receivers to recover from errors or remember sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Type codes tell the receiver whether a transaction carries data or control information. DTP leaves error recovery to the application protocol.
